extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students taking an algebraic geometry course (Math 216)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, basic properties, and key exercises about the intersection product (intersection number) of line bundles with coherent sheaves on projective varieties, together with related facts about elliptic-curve constructions and pathologies used as motivation and examples. The material includes the formal definition (20.1.1.1), multilinearity/symmetry, dependence on numerical equivalence, projection formula, asymptotic Riemann–Roch, and positivity for ample line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slicing criterion for regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the restriction of the cubic C to the line pq has three distinct (hence reduced, multiplicity 1) roots p, q, and r, then Cpq is regular at r, so r is a regular point of C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to deduce regularity of a point on C from regularity of its slice; see Exercise 12.2.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms determined by closed k-valued points
rubrics_metrics.description: Morphisms of varieties over k are determined by their behavior on closed (k-valued) points: two morphisms that agree on k-points are equal as morphisms of k-varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (Exercise 10.2.B) is used repeatedly to check equality of morphisms by checking maps on k-points and to glue morphisms constructed locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local construction of the third intersection point (Vieta formula criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given P=(P1,P2) and Q=(Q1,Q2) in an affine chart U0 with P1 ≠ Q1, the line PQ has equation x2 = m x1 + b (m and b rational functions of P,Q). Substituting into the cubic gives γ(x1)=A x1^3 + B x1^2 + C x1 + D; when A ≠ 0 (a Zariski-open condition), the third root is R1 := −B/A − P1 − Q1 and R2 = m R1 + b, yielding the third intersection point R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes a morphism tp,q on an open neighborhood of (p,q). The open conditions are P1 ≠ Q1 and A ≠ 0; these define the domain where the formula is valid and give the explicit rational functions defining the morphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluing local morphisms and descent by base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Local morphisms constructed on affine opens U[x1,x2] glue together because they agree after base change to the algebraic closure; two maps that are the same after base change to k̄ were the same to begin with (Exercise 9.2.I), so the locally defined maps produce a global k-morphism t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use agreement after base change plus Exercise 6.2.A (gluing morphisms) and Exercise 9.2.I (uniqueness after base change) to assemble globally defined morphisms defined over k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a k-linear form missing three points when |k| > 2
rubrics_metrics.description: If |k| > 2, there exists a linear form on P2 with coefficients in k that misses three given k-points P, Q, R (so some affine complements exist covering the required points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a small combinatorial/linear algebra assertion used to ensure coverage by affine opens; note it fails for k = F2 (Exercise 19.10.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of group variety structure on an elliptic curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an elliptic curve (E,p) embedded via |O_E(3p)|, define e: Spec k → E to be p, i: E → E by q ↦ t(p,q) (inverse), and m: E×E → E by (q,r) ↦ t(p, t(q,r)) (multiplication); these k-morphisms commute with arbitrary base extension and give (E,e,i,m) the structure of a group variety over k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To verify group axioms (identity, inverse, associativity) check equality of the relevant morphisms on k-points (Picard group computations yield equality on k-points) and conclude equality of morphisms by the 'morphisms determined by k-points' principle (Exercise 10.2.B); use base-change and Exercise 9.2.I to deduce the general k-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of multiplication-by-n map on an elliptic curve
rubrics_metrics.description: For an elliptic curve E, the multiplication-by-n map [n]: E → E has degree n^2 (heuristic from complex torus picture) and, in particular, for each n>0 the map [n] has positive degree, so there are only finitely many n-torsion points (Proposition 19.11.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction uses decomposition [n]=[2]∘[n/2] (degree multiplicative under composition) and counting arguments; see Exercise 19.11.6 and surrounding discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness/countability of torsion points and existence of non-torsion points over uncountable fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Each n-torsion subgroup is finite, so the union of torsion points is countable; over an uncountable algebraically closed field (e.g., C), an elliptic curve E has uncountably many closed points and hence must have non-torsion points (Corollary 19.11.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use degree results for [n] and cardinality arguments (double cover argument or counting x-values) to deduce existence of non-torsion points over uncountable fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for translations corresponding to graded-ring maps
rubrics_metrics.description: If E ⊂ P2 gives graded ring S•, a translation u: E → E corresponds to a map of (regraded) graded rings S• → S• if and only if u is translation by a torsion point; translation by a non-torsion point does not come from such a graded-ring map (Exercise 19.11.B / 19.11.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a test to detect whether a geometric automorphism arises from a map of graded rings; use the translation-by-torsion characterization when checking algebraicity at the graded-ring level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: intersection product / intersection number (20.1.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a coherent sheaf F with proper support of dimension ≤ n and invertible sheaves L1,...,Ln, define (L1⋯Ln · F) as the signed sum over all subsets of {1,...,n}: (−1)^m χ(X, L_{i1}^∨ ⊗ ... ⊗ L_{im}^∨ ⊗ F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When F = O_Y for a closed subscheme Y of dimension ≤ n, write (L1⋯Ln · Y). Note the notation convention: L^n does not mean L^{⊗n} but n factors of L appearing in the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection product is symmetric and multilinear (projective/proper case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For projective X and fixed coherent F, the intersection product (L1⋯Ln · F) is a symmetric multilinear function of the line bundles L1,...,Ln (Proposition 20.1.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses induction on n, the ability to write any line bundle as difference of two very ample bundles (Exercise 16.6.C), and existence of sections missing associated points (Exercise 18.6.A). Exercises 20.1.E–G guide the detailed steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection product preserved by field extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection product (L1⋯Ln · F) is preserved under extension of the base field (Exercise 20.1.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may therefore check many properties after base change to an infinite or algebraically closed field to simplify arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection with effective Cartier divisors reduces to restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is an effective Cartier divisor on X that restricts to an effective Cartier divisor D|Y on Y (or does not contain associated points of F), then (L1⋯Ln−1 · O(D) · Y) = (L1⋯Ln−1 · D|Y), and more generally (L1⋯O(D)·F) = (L1⋯·F|D) (Exercise 20.1.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows one to replace intersecting with the line bundle O(D) by intersecting with the Cartier divisor D and enables inductive arguments on dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing of (n+1)-fold intersections on too-small support
rubrics_metrics.description: If dim Supp F < n+1 then the intersection of n+1 invertible sheaves with F vanishes (Exercise 20.1.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This vanishing is used in deriving polynomiality of χ(X, L^m ⊗ F) and in other inductive arguments; it follows from the definition and dimension considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection product depends only on numerical equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: For projective X, the intersection product (L1⋯Ln · F) depends only on the numerical equivalence classes of the Li (Proposition 20.1.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multilinearity and reduction to the case where one Li is very ample and to effective Cartier divisors missing associated points of F, then apply the inductive hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic Riemann–Roch (leading coefficient as intersection number)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective, F coherent with dim Supp F ≤ n, and L a line bundle, then χ(X, L^{⊗m} ⊗ F) is a polynomial in m of degree ≤ n and the coefficient of m^n equals (L^n · F)/n! (Exercise 20.1.I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the vanishing exercise 20.1.H and expands the definition (20.1.1.1) to obtain recursion and leading-term identification; this generalizes curve Riemann–Roch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula for intersection numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X1 → X2 is a projective morphism of integral projective schemes of the same dimension n and L1,...,Ln are invertible sheaves on X2, then (π^*L1⋯π^*Ln) = deg(X1/X2)·(L1⋯Ln) (Exercise 20.1.J). More generally, for proper π and coherent F on X1 with dim Supp F ≤ n, (π^*L1⋯π^*Ln · F) = (L1⋯Ln · π_*F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to very ample case; choose sections whose intersection lies in an open where π is finite and flat of constant degree, and apply multiplicativity of degree and pushforward properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity when intersecting with an ample line bundle
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is projective and L is ample, then for any subvariety Y ⊂ X of dimension n, (L^n · Y) > 0 (Exercise 20.1.K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the very ample case and identify (L^n · Y) with degree of Y in the projective embedding induced by L; the Nakai–Moishezon criterion states the converse (positivity for all subvarieties characterizes ampleness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of very ample differences and sections missing associated points in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Key technical tools used throughout: every invertible sheaf can be written as the difference of two very ample line bundles (Exercise 16.6.C), and one can choose sections of very ample bundles missing associated points of a coherent sheaf (Exercise 18.6.A); these allow reduction to effective Cartier divisor cases and enable multilinearity and other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard proof techniques for intersection-theory statements such as multilinearity and dependence on numerical equivalence; the textbook cites Exercises 16.6.C and 18.6.A in the proofs.
